utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried exploration of one of the most ambitious novels in the English language.

Bleak House is Dickens at full stretch: a legal system that grinds lives to dust, a fog that never quite lifts, and a cast of characters whose fates are tangled in ways that take hundreds of pages to unravel.
Each episode, we take a theme, a scene, or a question — and we follow it wherever it leads.
Today we begin at the very beginning: fog, law, and fate — the three great atmospheres Dickens conjures in his opening chapters.
I'm joined by three wonderful readers, each of whom brings something distinct to the table.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class and power — and who will not let Dickens off lightly when the evidence demands otherwise.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don with a lifelong conviction that great fiction is, above all, a moral enterprise — and a withering eye for what he considers ideological overreach.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite recovered — which is, I think, the only proper response.
Let's begin with that opening — one of the most famous paragraphs in all of English prose.
Every time I return to those first pages, I'm struck by the sheer nerve of it.
Dickens doesn't ease you in — he drops you into the middle of something overwhelming and refuses to explain it.
The passage opens with just two words that function almost like a tolling bell.
"Fog everywhere."
And then it just keeps going — cascading, accumulating, refusing to stop.
The rhetorical trick is repetition — the word 'fog' appears so many times it stops being weather and becomes something more like fate.
And then there's this line, which I think is the one that catches you by the throat.
"Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little 'prentice boy on deck."
The fog doesn't merely obscure — it hurts people.
Caroline is right that the fog accumulates — but I think we should be precise about what it's accumulating around.
The pensioners, the skipper, the apprentice boy — these are not chosen randomly.
They are a careful social cross-section, and in every case the fog reaches those with the least power to escape it.
The skipper is wrathful — but it's the apprentice boy who suffers in the cold on deck.
Dickens sets up, in the very first paragraph, a world where suffering is distributed by social position.
The fog is atmosphere, yes — but it is also, already, an image of a system that crushes the people at the bottom.
Daniel makes a compelling case, as he always does.
But I would caution against reading the fog as a schematic diagram of class oppression — I think it does something rather more mysterious than that.
The passage ends, and this is the sentence that stays with me, with something genuinely vertiginous.
"Chance people on the bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the misty clouds."
These are not the exploited — they are simply people, lost.
The fog here is a condition of human existence — the fog of not knowing where you stand, or what is coming.
That is the fog Dickens is writing about — and no amount of class analysis quite captures it.
I think Edmund and Daniel are both right — and I'm not sure those two readings are as opposed as they might seem.
The fog is moral and material at once — it is the atmosphere of Chancery, which is both a legal institution and a spiritual condition.
And then, by such a strange contrast, there's what Esther finds when she arrives at Bleak House itself — and I always find this almost shocking, how different it feels.
She describes it like this — and I want to read it because the rhythm of the sentence is part of what it means.

"With its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House."
That 'just wind enough without' — that tiny qualification — is exactly right.
The outside world still exists — it just can't get in.
That passage is genuinely beautiful — and I'd be churlish to deny it.
But the warmth of Bleak House is only intelligible against the fog outside — it depends on the suffering it excludes.
Jarndyce's generosity is real — Dickens means us to feel it.
But his comfort is the product of a world whose cruelty we've just been shown in that opening fog.
The novel won't let you simply enjoy the warmth — the fog is still out there, pinching the fingers of the apprentice boy.
I don't disagree that the contrast is deliberate — Dickens is far too skilled a craftsman for such things to be accidental.
But what strikes me about the Bleak House description is that it is Esther who is speaking — and that matters enormously.
Esther has known very little warmth in her life — and so her capacity to receive it, her gratitude for it, is itself a moral quality.
The furniture, the quaint portraits, the rose-leaves in the drawers — these are not symbols of bourgeois exclusion.
They are the texture of a home that someone has cared for — and Esther, for the first time, is inside it.
And it's from Edmund's point — Esther inside a place of warmth — that I want to turn to its shadow.
Because the novel has another house — Chesney Wold — and over that house hangs a curse that is everything Bleak House is not.
There's a woman in the novel's backstory — a crippled lady, proud and silent — who has spent her last days walking the terrace at Chesney Wold.
Her husband has wronged her — the novel doesn't labour the point — and she has refused, on any persuasion, to speak to him since.
And when she finally falls, and he comes to help her, she says this — and I find it one of the most chilling speeches in the novel.

"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
She is already dying — and she is already promising to haunt.
The fog outside, the ghost at the terrace — this novel is saturated with forces that will not be contained.
That passage is extraordinary precisely because it is not Gothic decoration — it is a portrait of will.
She never complained, we are told — never spoke to anyone of being crippled or in pain.
And then at the last moment, the will speaks — not in self-pity, but in prophecy.
This is what great novelists can do — they make fate feel like character.
Edmund's reading is elegant — but I want to press on the word 'pride.'
The curse is not simply aimed at this one man — it is aimed at the house, at the family, at an institution of aristocratic power.
'Let the Dedlocks listen for my step' — she doesn't say 'let him' or 'let you.'
The curse is systemic — it falls on the dynasty, the bloodline, the name.
And if you think of what actually happens to Lady Dedlock by the novel's end, you begin to feel the weight of that prophecy.
Fog, warmth, and a ghost who walks in her grave — and we are barely inside the first chapters.
What I love about this conversation is how the novel refuses to resolve into a single atmosphere — it holds them all at once.
In our next segment, we'll follow the fog into Chancery itself — the legal institution that sits at the heart of everything.
Do stay with us.

segments.title: The Machinery of Injustice: Chancery and Class

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great fog-bound novel apart — chapter by chapter, brick by brick — to see what it's actually made of.
Today's segment is called The Machinery of Injustice: Chancery and Class.
We're asking how this novel anatomises power — how the law, the aristocracy, and the institutions of Victorian England grind their most vulnerable inhabitants to dust.
Joining me today are three readers who know this novel intimately and disagree about it in productive ways.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — every institution, for Daniel, is a mechanism that protects the rich and destroys the poor.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's genius lies in moral imagination, not social programme — and who will keep the rest of us honest.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read Bleak House more times than she can count, and whose ear for Dickens's verbal music is second to none.
Let's begin with the novel's darkest rooms — the ones that smell of tallow and opium.
What strikes me most about the novel's social critique is how Dickens locates it in the body.
Not in argument, not in polemic — in flesh and furniture.
When Tulkinghorn enters Nemo's room, Dickens doesn't give us a speech about poverty.
He gives us a candle that has guttered down so far its wick has doubled over — a tower of winding-sheet above it.
And then — this is the sentence I keep returning to — he describes the sensation of the room entering the lawyer's own body.
"through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium."
The poverty doesn't stay on the other side of the threshold — it gets into Tulkinghorn's mouth.
That is a radical act of imagination, and Dickens probably didn't know how radical it was.
Daniel, I won't dispute the vividness of that passage — it is extraordinary.
But I think you misread what Dickens is doing with Tulkinghorn here.
The detail of the taste entering the lawyer's mouth is not a political metaphor — it is characterisation.
Dickens is placing us inside a legal mind that registers the world in surfaces and sensations — never in sympathy.
Tulkinghorn tastes opium but feels nothing — and that is precisely the moral indictment.
I want to hold both of those readings, because I think Dickens earns both of them simultaneously.
But what moves me in that passage is actually the description of Nemo himself.
"His hair is ragged, mingling with his whiskers and his beard — the latter, ragged too, and grown, like the scum and mist around him, in neglect."
The man and the room have become one thing.
He has grown into his surroundings — or been dissolved into them.
And there is something unbearable about that — about a human being so reduced that he merges with scum and mist.
And who is Nemo? Nobody. That is what his name means, and that is what the system has made him.
But Dickens does something quietly devastating with Jo's testimony about this man.
Jo tells us that one cold winter night, when the boy was shivering in a doorway, Nemo turned back to look at him.
And having questioned him and found that he had not a friend in the world, said —
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
Two people with nothing — and one of them gives.
The state gives nothing. The law gives nothing. The anonymous, dissolving poor man gives what he has.
That is genuinely moving, and I would not for a moment reduce it to sociology.
What Dickens is giving us there is a study in natural grace — the goodness that survives in a man whom the world has entirely stripped of position and respectability.
The narrator confirms this with characteristic directness in the passage about Jo.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
A distant ray of light — that is a carefully calibrated theological image.
Dickens does not say Jo is saved. He says there is something like a ray.
The misspelling — 'wery good' — that is not condescension. That is Dickens's tenderness in its purest form.
I always read that passage aloud when I want to remind myself why I love this novel.
But I want to bring in Mrs. Piper, because Dickens won't let us be sentimental for long.
Right alongside Jo's heartbreaking testimony, we have this magnificent torrent of neighbourhood gossip.
"Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
That single sentence is one of the funniest structural jokes in the novel.
And then Dickens actually reproduces the experience — the syntax falls apart, the parentheses breed more parentheses.
It is funny and it is damning — because this is the community's evidence, and it amounts to nothing.
Exactly — and notice who is allowed to give evidence and who is not.
Mrs. Piper testifies at length. Jo is a rejected witness — legally incompetent, unable to take the oath.
The inquest gives the floor to rambling hearsay and closes it to the one person who actually knew the dead man.
That is not a coincidence in Dickens — that is the system performing exactly as designed.
And yet Chancery's violence isn't only visited on the anonymous poor — it permeates the aristocratic world of Chesney Wold as well.
Daniel, you wanted to talk about the ghost story that Mrs. Rouncewell tells — the original Lady Dedlock, the woman who lamed herself in the stables.
Yes — because that story is usually read as gothic atmosphere, and I think that reading is correct as far as it goes but doesn't go far enough.
What is the original Lady Dedlock actually doing in those stables?
She is committing sabotage. She is laming the horses of a Royalist family — in direct service of the Parliamentary cause.
Mrs. Rouncewell tells it as a ghost story — but the ghost's original act was political resistance.
And the consequence is devastating, set up with that terrible economy Dickens gives the housekeeper:
"she was lamed in the hip and from that hour began to pine away."
From that hour — not gradually, not eventually. From that hour.
The punishment for defiance is permanent physical damage, and it begins immediately.
I think you're importing a political framework that Mrs. Rouncewell — and Dickens — simply don't intend.
The story as told is one of a marriage gone catastrophically wrong — a lady of haughty temper, a husband ill-suited to her in age and character, no children to moderate between them.
The civil war gives the hatred a focus, but the hatred was already there.
What Dickens anatomises here is not class — it is the destructive capacity of pride when it has nowhere to go.
What I find extraordinary is how Mrs. Rouncewell's cadence itself carries the tragedy.
Dickens writes that she 'gravely nods and continues' — that gravity is doing enormous work.
She is not dramatising — she is reciting. This is inherited knowledge, kept in the house like the furniture.
And that connects it to the later story Jarndyce tells about Lady Dedlock's sister — the living sacrifice.
Both women are destroyed by a combination of their own pride and the rigid codes of the world they live in.
The Jarndyce passage is the one that haunts me most in this segment — because it names the mechanism with such terrible precision.
Lady Dedlock's sister doesn't simply decide to renounce Boythorn. She writes him a letter.
And in that letter she enacts a kind of legal self-annihilation — listen to how Jarndyce describes it:

"she wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did — and that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too."
'Exacted' — that is the word. The sacrifice is not freely given. It is extracted.
His proud temper and strained honour demand it. Her own pride — that same code internalised — confirms it.
The ideology doesn't need to coerce her from outside — she has already made it her own.
Daniel, I'll grant you 'exacted' — it is a remarkable word choice and you are right to press it.
But the sentence continues — and this is what makes Dickens a great novelist rather than a pamphleteer.
"In consideration for those master points in him, and even in consideration for them in herself, she made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it."
She claims the sacrifice as her own — 'she said.' Dickens preserves her agency within her catastrophe.
That is not ideology. That is character — the most pitiless and sympathetic kind of character study.
And Jarndyce ends with the loneliest sentence — 'Nor did any one.'
He never saw her. He never heard of her from that hour. And nobody else did either.
She vanished completely — she made herself into a nobody, in the same way the system made Nemo into a nobody.
I think that is the thread — voluntary self-erasure and forced self-erasure are mirror images in this novel.
Voluntary and forced self-erasure as mirror images — that is a thought I want to carry into our next segment.

We've been tracing the machinery of injustice through aristocratic ghostlore, through a dead law-writer's squalid room, and through Jo — the boy who can't give evidence but who, in Dickens's hands, gives us more moral clarity than any courtroom.
After the break, we'll turn to Esther Summerson — and ask whether the novel's most celebrated voice is also its most troubling one.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most sustained acts of moral observation — the world Esther and Ada enter when they accompany Mrs. Pardiggle to the brickmakers' cottages.
And from there, we follow the long shadow that falls over Richard Carstone and Ada Clare as they move through the novel toward its darker country.
With me today are three people whose company I'm always glad of when the material gets this serious.
Sir Edmund Leigh, whose deep patience with the novel's moral architecture makes him an indispensable guide to its quieter devastations.
Dr. Daniel Rosen, who reads every institution in this novel as a mechanism — and is characteristically honest about what it produces.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has lived inside this novel long enough to know exactly where it hurts.
Edmund, let's begin with the brickmaker — because the moment Dickens gives him the floor, everything changes.
Indeed it does, and one ought to pause before it.
Mrs. Pardiggle arrives with her notebooks and her tract, fully armoured in the certainties of philanthropic purpose.
And the brickmaker strips every one of those certainties from her — not with argument, but with testimony.
He anticipates her questions and answers them himself, with a kind of terrible preemptive ferocity.
Dickens gives him the words, and one feels the full weight of what those words contain.
"Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks. How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead!"
And then the full catalogue — the dirt, the disease, the dead children — delivered with the same scorching logic.
"We've had five dirty and onwholesome children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them, and for us besides."
That line ought to stop the reader entirely.
It is not sentiment — it is a man who has reasoned his way to a conclusion that polite society cannot afford to hear.
Edmund is right to call it testimony, though I'd push further — it's an indictment.
What the brickmaker performs is the complete failure of the charitable model — he names every element of his degradation and traces it back to material conditions.
The water is undrinkable. His children are dead. His wife has a bruise from his own hand — and he names that too, with horrible candour.
Mrs. Pardiggle brings books fit for a baby, as he puts it — and the novel agrees with him.
Dickens is showing us that charity, as an institution, is designed to manage the poor — not to alter the conditions that create poverty.
The tract cannot compete with contaminated water. The little book cannot feed five dead children.
And then — almost immediately — the baby dies in its mother's arms while Ada reaches toward it.
Esther narrates it in four words: "The child died."
"As she did so, I saw what happened and drew her back. The child died."
The compression is devastating. Dickens refuses to elaborate because the fact requires no ornamentation.
I've read that scene many times, and those four words never lose their force.
What strikes me as much as the death is what Esther does with the handkerchief afterwards.
She raises it to look at the sleeping child, she sees the light through Ada's hair bent over in pity — and then Dickens reaches forward across the whole novel.
The passage is extraordinary in what it asks the reader to hold simultaneously — tenderness and foreboding.
"How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the child through Ada's drooping hair as her pity bent her head—"
"—how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!"
That word — unquiet — does so much work.
The dead infant's breast is peaceful. The living woman who will later carry that cloth is anything but.
Dickens has planted a seed of grief in a scene of grief, and most readers don't even know it yet.
The handkerchief is one of the novel's finest examples of what I would call providential plotting — the object that links fates across the novel's span.
And yet what strikes me equally in these early chapters is the contrast between that world of the brickmakers and the world of sunlit rooms through which Ada and Richard pass.
Dickens gives them a moment of almost unbearable loveliness, and then he clouds it.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
"Passed away" — even the phrasing carries it. These are not figures moving toward brightness; they are moving toward dissolution.
And Dickens has the restraint to let a cloud do the work that a lesser novelist would have done with exposition.
That passage is stunning, and I don't want to diminish its beauty — but I think we have to ask what Richard is walking into.
Richard's destruction is not a private tragedy of character — it is Chancery at work on a young man.
The court gives him just enough hope to keep him investing — his time, his health, his capacity to commit to any other life.
He is not weak so much as he is trapped — and the trap wears the face of the law.
The sunlight Dickens gives them in that corridor is real — Richard's hope is real — and that is precisely what makes the system so cruel.
And Ada watches him go, and she keeps watching, and she stays.
What I find almost unbearable in that passage is that she is looking up at his face and seems to see nothing else.
She is not deceived — she simply loves him. And love in this novel is not a shelter; it is an exposure.
The same novel that shows us a dead infant in a brickmaker's hovel shows us those two walking into shadow — and asks us to feel both losses as part of the same world.
I want to bring in two more figures before we close — Bucket and Sir Leicester — because together they open something unexpected in the novel's moral register.
Edmund, Bucket's appeal to Jarndyce — give Esther to me, or Lady Dedlock may not survive — is one of the great coercive speeches in Dickens.
Bucket is perhaps the most carefully observed professional in the novel — he calculates everything, including his own sincerity.
And yet in that speech, the calculation and the genuine urgency are inseparable.
He frames every second as a financial loss — an hour is worth a hundred pounds, then a thousand — which is the language of the commercial world.
But underneath the accounting there is something that sounds almost like fear — for her.
"If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation."

"But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for — I ask no question, and I say no more than that — she will give me credit for being friendly."
"I ask no question" — that is Bucket at his most tactful and his most manipulative simultaneously.
He knows everything and pretends to know nothing, so that Jarndyce and Esther may do what he needs them to do of their own apparent free will.
Bucket is the novel's most fascinating servant of the state — he belongs entirely to the world of detection and control, and yet Dickens makes him sympathetic.
That tension is real. He is trying to save Lady Dedlock — but he is also the mechanism by which she is pursued.
The fact that he frames her danger in terms of monetary value — each hour worth a hundred pounds — tells us something about the world that employs him.
Compassion and commerce have become indistinguishable, and Dickens is quite clear-eyed about that.
And then Sir Leicester, which for me is one of the novel's most quietly astonishing passages.
For much of the novel he is a figure of gentle satire — his baronetcy, his precedents, his constitutional horror at anything new.
And then his wife's secret is exposed, and he rises to meet it with something that the novel can only call honour.
The narrator offers a judgment that I find genuinely moving — it levels all distinctions of class in a single sentence.
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
Children of the dust — it takes in everyone. The brickmaker's dead infants and the baronet in his great house.
Dickens arrives at his most democratic statement through his most aristocratic character — and I don't think that's accidental.
Caroline has put her finger on something essential — Dickens does not redeem Sir Leicester by making him less of a Tory.
He redeems him by showing that his fidelity and his gallantry — those old-fashioned virtues — are exactly what the moment requires.
The novel says his conquest of his own wrong and his own pride for her sake is simply honourable, manly, and true.
That word simply does remarkable work — it strips away all the social scaffolding and leaves only the moral fact.
I have always felt that Dickens was more conservative in his bones than his admirers care to acknowledge, and Sir Leicester is the evidence.
I'd say rather that Dickens is exposing the contradiction — a man whose class values have denied humanity to countless others can only redeem himself by acting against those same values.
Sir Leicester's grace is real, but it doesn't rehabilitate the system he embodies. Dickens knows that too.
The brickmaker's children are still dead. The water is still undrinkable.
Edmund's conservative Dickens and Daniel's radical Dickens — and somehow the novel contains both, which is perhaps why we're still here arguing about it.
Caroline, the last word — in a novel full of shadows closing over young people, what do you hold onto?
I hold onto that halo that Esther sees shining through Ada's drooping hair.
It's not a sentimental image — it's an act of attention. Esther is watching, and recording, and refusing to look away.
And she ends that passage with the woman at the door — not Ada, not herself, but Jenny — saying over and over, in her old soothing manner, "Jenny, Jenny."
That small, repeated name, at the edge of grief — that is what I hold onto.
Edmund Leigh, Daniel Rosen, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you. This has been Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll be back with more from this extraordinary novel — a world Dickens built with equal parts fury and tenderness, and which repays every hour we spend inside it.

segments.title: Secrets and Shadows: Lady Dedlock Unmasked

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we read Dickens's great fog-bound novel with the attention it demands.
I'm your host, and today we are deep inside the novel's architecture of secrets — the locked rooms, the withheld names, the faces that reveal nothing.
With me are three readers who know this novel very well.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel — every lawyer, every patron — as a mechanism of class power.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's genius is moral and human, not political — and he will tell you so with great courtesy.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read Bleak House more times than she will admit, and cares passionately about how every sentence sounds.
Today's segment is about concealment — what these characters hide, and what the novel itself withholds from us.
Edmund, let's begin with Tulkinghorn, because Dickens gives him one of the most extraordinary descriptions in the whole book.
Yes, and it is a description that rewards very slow reading indeed.
Dickens gives us Tulkinghorn standing aloof by an old portmanteau — physically present, yet somehow entirely absent.
He has witnessed a death — a destitute man's death — and shown nothing.
Neither patience nor impatience, the narrator tells us.
"He has shown neither patience nor impatience, nor attention nor abstraction. He has shown nothing but his shell."
That word — shell — is precise and devastating.
It implies that there may be no interior to speak of — or that whatever interior exists is permanently inaccessible.
And then Dickens offers the analogy that I think is among the most brilliant in the novel.
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
The pun on case — instrument case, legal case — is working very hard there.
Dickens is not merely describing a man but describing a kind of ontological problem: the impossibility of knowing another person who has chosen absolute self-enclosure.
Edmund, that pun stopped me the first time I read the passage as a teenager, and it stops me still.
There is something almost comic about it — and then suddenly it isn't comic at all.
Because what Dickens is saying, beneath the wit, is that this man is unknowable by design.
He has made himself into an instrument of concealment, not just a keeper of secrets but a secret himself.
And later chapters confirm this with a kind of gothic grandeur when Tulkinghorn arrives at Chesney Wold.
The description is extraordinary — he comes at his usual methodical pace, which is never quickened, never slackened.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb, every crease — the secrets have physically colonised him.
That image of secrets in every crease is not just gothic atmosphere — it is a description of function.
Tulkinghorn's body is, in a very literal sense, the archive of the ruling class.
He holds what the aristocracy cannot afford to have spoken aloud.
And Dickens asks the question that really matters: whose interests does this devotion serve?
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
Services he sells — that is the key phrase.
Tulkinghorn is not a loyal retainer elevated by devotion; he is a professional, a commodity broker in other people's shame.
The aristocracy needs him because it cannot govern itself without concealment — that is the structural function of a lawyer like Tulkinghorn in Dickens's world.
Daniel, I take the point about professional function, and I will not argue with it entirely.
But what I find more disturbing — and more interesting — is the moral vacancy.
The narrator says he is his own client in the matter of his soul, and will never betray himself.
This is not a villain who rationalises his villainy — he has simply removed the question of conscience from the frame entirely.
And that, to my mind, is the more terrifying portrait — not the system, but the individual who has chosen to become its instrument.
And the information Tulkinghorn is carrying toward Lady Dedlock is the match that will light the fuse.
Sir Leicester reads the message aloud, seemingly unaware of what it means — and that scene is almost unbearably tense.
Caroline, do you want to take us through that moment?
It is a scene that Dickens engineers with absolute precision, and the comedy of Sir Leicester fumbling for his eyeglass is doing real work.
We are told that my Lady looks a little irritated — and we as readers know that irritation is covering something far more dangerous.
And then Sir Leicester reads Tulkinghorn's message, stumbling through it — and he finally lands on the sentence that detonates everything.
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words — I have seen him — and Lady Dedlock's carefully maintained world begins to fracture.
Sir Leicester is entirely innocent of what he is saying.
He thinks he is relaying a social pleasantry from the family solicitor.
The gap between what he understands and what we understand is one of the most painful ironies in the whole novel.
And what Tulkinghorn has seen, of course, is not merely a person — he has seen a vulnerability, and he intends to use it.
This is the mechanism by which powerful men — lawyers, in Dickens's world — maintain their dominance over even aristocratic clients.
Knowledge is leverage.
Lady Dedlock has rank and wealth, but Tulkinghorn holds the document — and the document is power.
What Dickens is showing us, structurally, is that the legal system is not the neutral guardian of the truth — it is a machine for accumulating leverage over people.
I would add something about what Lady Dedlock's secret actually is — because the secrecy around Esther's identity is presented to us through a passage I find rather affecting.
Mr. Jarndyce recounts to Esther the extraordinarily guarded communication he received from the woman who turns out to be her mother.
The woman will not be seen, will not give her name.
She yields only this — and Jarndyce quotes it almost verbatim.

"That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
The steadfastness of her resolution — that phrase is not condemnation, it is almost admiration.
Here is a woman, utterly alone, protecting what she can protect, at terrible cost to herself.
That is not a political condition — it is a human one.
Edmund, that reading moves me — and I want to add to it.
What is so quietly devastating in the passage is the phrase — her name was an assumed one.
Even the name she hides behind is not her name.
She has built a self entirely composed of concealment, and she cannot stop.
Jarndyce's closing line to Esther — my dear, I have told you all — is heartbreaking precisely because it is the opposite of the truth.
He has told her almost nothing, because almost nothing is what he has.
And yet the system of secrecy is not only romantic tragedy — it is also professional procedure, and Dickens shows us that too.
Vholes — Richard's lawyer — is one of the most quietly monstrous figures in the book.
He performs openness as a kind of weapon.
He tells Esther that he noted his exact words in his diary — producible at any time, he says — and then delivers the most devastating possible verdict on Richard's affairs.
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account."
I will not smooth things over — but the smoothing is precisely what he does, and has been doing, as he methodically destroys Richard.
He calls it professional duty — I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one.
That last clause — though it can be charged to no one — is the comedy of the law in Bleak House in a single phrase.
The grotesquerie of Vholes is that he is scrupulously correct — there is no specific lie one can identify.
And then, in the very next breath, he turns to greet Richard as though the conversation had been perfectly agreeable.
Enjoying the pleasure of some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson — the phrase makes one shudder.
It is the smile of the predator, rendered in perfect social form.
What this conversation reveals is how thoroughly Bleak House is a novel about the uses of opacity — for the powerful, for the desperate, and for the merely professional.
Tulkinghorn carries secrets in his every crease; Lady Dedlock builds an entire identity from what she will not say; Vholes conceals ruin behind procedural candour.
In the next segment, we'll turn to what happens when those secrets begin — slowly, inevitably — to surface.

segments.title: Bleak House Comedy: Eccentricity and Hope

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great fog-bound novel apart sentence by sentence — and puts it back together as something even richer.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at something that often gets overshadowed by the novel's darkness: its comedy.
The eccentricity, the satire, the moments of absurdist delight that run like a bright thread through all that fog and mud.
With me today are three exceptional readers of this novel.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel — the law, the aristocracy, philanthropy — as a mechanism of power, and finds Dickens more radical than Dickens himself may have realised.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's genius is moral, not political — and who brings to every reading an enviable precision of ear and judgment.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite recovered — in the best possible sense.
She'll be our guide today into what Dickens does when he's being funny — and why it matters.
Caroline, let's start at the very beginning — the novel's opening, which is one of the most extraordinary paragraphs in all of English fiction.
It is, isn't it — and the thing that strikes me every single time I re-read it is that it's funny before it's anything else.
Dickens opens this enormous novel — this vast anatomy of English society — with mud.
And then, before you've quite settled into the grimness of it, he drops something completely surreal into the sentence.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A Megalosaurus. Waddling. Up Holborn Hill.
The sheer absurdity of that image — the specificity of "forty feet long or so" — is comic genius dressed up as apocalyptic vision.
And it sets you completely off-balance, which is exactly where Dickens wants you for the next nine hundred pages.
Caroline is right to call it comic, though I'd want to be precise about what kind of comedy it is.
It is not the comedy of incongruity for its own sake — Dickens is not simply being whimsical.
That prehistoric creature waddling through London is a moral image: this is a world so sunk in primordial muck that civilisation itself feels provisional.
Consider what follows: the smoke makes "a soft black drizzle," and Dickens remarks — with perfect deadpan — that it has "gone into mourning for the death of the sun."
The comedy and the elegy are inseparable — which is, I'd argue, the mark of a truly great prose stylist.
Dickens is not writing satire because he despairs. He is writing satire because he still cares.
I'll accept that Edmund, though I'd push it further.
The comedy here is doing something structurally important: it establishes from the very first paragraph that this is a world in decay, and that the decay is systemic.
Look at that phrase — mud accumulating at compound interest.
"Adding new deposits to the crust upon crust of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and accumulating at compound interest."
Compound interest. In the mud. On the first page of the novel.
Dickens is telling you immediately that the logic of capital has infected the very ground under people's feet.
The comedy is the delivery mechanism — the absurdity gets you laughing, and then the logic lands.
And that comic logic runs all the way through the novel's treatment of class, doesn't it.
The passage about Lady Dedlock in Chapter Two is one of my absolute favourites — because it exposes the whole machinery of aristocratic fashion with such gleeful precision.
Lady Dedlock believes herself to be — and this is Dickens's phrase — "an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals."
And yet every tradesperson, every dressmaker, every librarian has her completely figured out and leads her around by the nose.
Here's the image Dickens uses for how they do it — and it's extraordinary.
"Who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
Lady Dedlock as a miniature fleet — stately, majestic, and utterly captive.
The wit of it is almost cruel, but it's so perfect you can't help laughing.
The Gulliver comparison is inspired, yes — though I'd note that Dickens is careful not to make Lady Dedlock simply ridiculous.
She has genuine dignity, genuine tragedy. The comedy here is directed at the system that produces her — the world of Blaze and Sparkle, Sheen and Gloss.
Those names alone — "Blaze and Sparkle," "Sheen and Gloss" — are perfect satirical invention.
They convey exactly how the aristocracy constructs its own magnificence through the eager labour of commerce.
Dickens is a moralist here as much as a satirist — he shows you the folly without stripping the subject of her humanity.
That's well put, Edmund, though I think the comedy in the Snagsby passage is even sharper — because the satire there has no mercy whatsoever.
Dickens takes the marriage relation — that supposedly sacred bond — and renders it as pure surveillance.
Mrs. Snagsby becomes literally a shadow — inescapable, omnipresent, and the language Dickens uses is savage in its irony.
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."
And then the punchline arrives in the language of the marriage service itself.
"Bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow."
"Till death do us part" has become "till secrecy is impossible."
It's comic, but it's also a precise critique of how domestic power operates.
That passage stops me every time — because the rhythm of it is so hypnotic.
"Shadow of his shadow" — three words and a whole marriage portrait.
But I want to bring in the Smallweed scene, because Bucket's whispered commentary there is some of the funniest writing in the novel.
Bucket has this stained, singed will — practically rescued from a fireplace — and he whispers to Jarndyce the whole sordid backstory of the Smallweed family in about four sentences.
The compression of it is extraordinary — a whole family's moral portrait in a breath.
"There ain't one of the family that wouldn't sell the other for a pound or two, except the old lady — and she's only out of it because she's too weak in her mind to drive a bargain."
That last clause — "too weak in her mind to drive a bargain" — is both devastating and gloriously funny.
It's the one mercy in the Smallweed universe, and it's purely accidental.
What Bucket achieves in that whisper is something only the very best comic novelists manage — moral judgment delivered as casual observation.
He is not raging at the Smallweeds. He is simply noting them, with something close to professional amusement.
And that restraint is what makes it land so hard.
The comedy throughout this novel works because Dickens never explains the joke.
He trusts his readers to be intelligent — which is, in itself, a form of respect not always found in popular fiction.
I'd add one more register of comedy that I think gets undervalued — the hope that flickers through even the darkest satire.
There's a passage from Mrs. Badger about Richard Carstone's failure to commit to medicine — and what she says about Woodcourt in contrast is quietly extraordinary.
She sets up the counterimage of vocation — what it looks like when someone actually means their work.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
This isn't comedy exactly — but it's the thing that gives the comedy its weight.
The novel's satire is so devastating precisely because Dickens can also imagine what genuine commitment looks like.
The jokes are funny because the alternative is real.
That's a beautiful place to pause — the idea that the comedy and the hope are not opposites but the same instrument played in different keys.
We've moved from a Megalosaurus waddling up Holborn Hill to Woodcourt's quiet endurance — which is actually the full range of this novel.
My thanks to Daniel, Edmund, and Caroline for a conversation that's done what good literary talk always should — sent me straight back to the book.
In our next segment, we turn to the darkness behind the laughter — what the fog really means, and what it costs the people who live inside it.

segments.title: Narrative Mirrors: How Dickens Tells His Tale

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with real pleasure.
Today's segment looks at how Dickens tells his story — the narrative architecture he uses to put secrets, self-deception, and moral drift on the page.
Joining me are three guests who know this novel extremely well and who see it, I think it's fair to say, from rather different angles.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Dickens as an anatomist of class power — every lawyer, every lord, every charitable institution is, for Daniel, a mechanism.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes Dickens's genius is moral rather than political — a novelist of individual character tested to its limits.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who came to Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite left — she is here above all to make us hear the prose.
The novel has two narrators — Esther Summerson in the first person, and an unnamed omniscient voice in the present tense.
Let's begin with that omniscient narrator — because there are passages in Chapters Twelve and Thirteen where Dickens does something quite extraordinary with point of view.
What strikes me every time I re-read those Chesney Wold scenes is how ruthlessly controlled the prose is.
Dickens gives us Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn meeting day after day — and the surface is perfectly polished.
Listen to how he describes them — I want to read this because the rhythm does half the work.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
"Mr. Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
Those two portraits sit side by side like paired daguerreotypes — each one a mask, each one a study in concealment.
And then Dickens pulls the rug away entirely — with that extraordinary sentence about what neither of them will ever know about the other.
Caroline puts her finger on something essential, I think — though I'd frame it rather differently.
What Dickens is doing here is not a structural trick — it is a moral observation about the human capacity for self-enclosure.
These two people have sealed themselves so completely behind their social roles that even the narrator cannot penetrate them.
The passage from Chapter Twelve makes this explicit, I think, with a kind of forensic precision.

"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows."
"All this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
That phrase — for the time — is where the tragedy is concentrated.
It is the narrator quietly telling us that this concealment cannot last — that revelation is already approaching, whether they know it or not.
Edmund is right about the tragedy — though I think we need to ask whose interests that concealment serves.
Tulkinghorn is not hiding out of shame or love — he is hoarding information as a form of power.
Dickens calls him a repository of noble confidences — which is a brilliantly precise description of how the legal profession functions in this novel.
The confidences belong to the nobility — but the power over those confidences belongs to Tulkinghorn.
And notice what Sir Leicester does throughout all this watching — he looks at the fire.
Dickens tells us he looks at the fire, quote, with the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.
He is an ancestor portrait — inert, decorative, watching nothing, understanding less.
That is Dickens's verdict on the aristocracy in three words: the Dedlock on the staircase.
That image of Sir Leicester and the fire is one of the funniest things in the book — and also one of the most devastating.
But I want to stay with the present tense for a moment, because it's doing something formally very strange.
The omniscient narrator speaks in the present tense — have looked, meet again, are always — as if events are happening as we read.
It gives the surveillance a relentless, ongoing quality — as if neither character is ever allowed a moment off.
They meet again at dinner — again, next day — again, for many days in succession.
That repetition — again, again, again — is almost hypnotic, like a clock that won't stop ticking.
Which brings us, naturally, to the Esther chapters — where the register shifts completely.
In Chapter Thirteen we have Mr. Jarndyce speaking to Richard — and this is intimate, warm, pastoral in its way.
Jarndyce's advice to Richard is, I think, one of the great pieces of moral instruction in English fiction.
He tells the boy, and I find this worth reading at length —
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
"Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
"If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it."
That is not ideology — that is wisdom.
And it is rendered all the more poignant because we, as readers, already sense Richard won't heed it.
I'd agree with Edmund on the poignancy — though I'd push back gently on calling it simple wisdom.
Jarndyce is telling Richard that Providence and personal effort are sufficient — that the world is before you and will receive you as you enter it.
But Richard's problem isn't a lack of effort or constancy in the abstract — it is Chancery.
By Chapter Twenty-Three, Richard himself articulates this with painful clarity — he confesses to Esther in a moment of complete honesty.
"I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow — but constant to myself."

"If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt."
Richard knows the language of moral failure — and he applies it to himself faithfully.
But Dickens has been showing us all along that the institution he is ensnared in is specifically designed to produce this kind of dissolution.
Jarndyce's advice is good counsel — for a world where Chancery doesn't exist.
What moves me about Richard's confession is the way he trails off — that dash at the end.
Esther, as narrator, records it faithfully — and shouldn't be in debt, and — and then nothing.
The sentence doesn't complete because Richard can't complete it — he doesn't know what comes after the debt.
And Esther's narration — unlike the omniscient narrator — won't fill in what she can't see.
That's the formal genius of the dual narration — each voice has its own limit, its own blind spot.
The omniscient narrator can see into Tulkinghorn's social mask — but admits he cannot penetrate the hidden heart.
Esther can record Richard's words precisely — but can't imagine what lies ahead of him.
Together they make a picture of the world — but it is always, in some essential way, incomplete.
That word — incomplete — feels like exactly the right note on which to pause.
Two narrators, each seeing sharply and each seeing partially — and the novel living in the space between them.
We'll come back to what that structural choice costs and what it gains, after we look more closely at the characters who have to carry the novel's most painful knowledge.

segments.title: Closing: The Weight of Systems, the Light of Care

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the great architecture of Bleak House — its fog, its law, its suffering.
But I want to close by sitting with two very different kinds of scene that the novel holds in balance.
On one side, Jo — the crossing-sweeper, barely a name, barely a self — testifying in a coroner's court.
On the other, a warm domestic evening at Bleak House — Richard, Ada, and Esther, hearts full of early love.
Daniel, you've been wanting to get to Jo all episode. The floor is yours.
The Jo passage is one of the most devastating things Dickens ever wrote.
It's written in this brutal catechism form — question, non-answer, question, non-answer.
Every question the court asks reveals another thing society has withheld from this child.
Listen to what Dickens strips it down to:
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Six words of biography. Six words that are an indictment of the entire social order.
And then — and this is the twist of the knife — Jo still believes in moral truth.
He knows it's wicked to tell a lie. He simply doesn't know who taught him that — or why the world that taught him has given him nothing in return.
I won't quarrel with a word of that. The passage destroys the reader — as it is meant to.
But I'd locate the genius slightly differently.
What Dickens has done is give Jo a moral imagination that the court — and the society it represents — is incapable of recognising.
Jo cannot spell his name. He can scarcely articulate his own existence.
And yet he will tell the truth, because — in his own words — "it'll be something wery bad to punish him" if he doesn't, "and serve him right."
There is a moral seriousness in that boy that puts the court entirely to shame.
Daniel calls it systemic. I call it a portrait of innate human dignity resisting erasure.
What undoes me about that passage is the rhythm of the negatives.
No. Never. Don't. Can't. Every sentence is a door closing.
And then you turn the page and there's Esther, sitting between Richard and Ada, all warmth and candlelight.
Dickens places these scenes in the same novel deliberately, and the contrast is almost unbearable.
Esther describes that evening with Richard and Ada — she sets up the quote so beautifully herself:
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That little aside — 'I enjoyed it too much myself' — that's Esther in one breath.
Selfless, warm, and just quietly, privately happy.
The contrast Caroline identifies is structural, not accidental.
Esther's world at Bleak House operates on the logic of care — mutual, reciprocal, freely given.
Jo's world operates on the logic of indifference — institutional, systematic, total.
And Dickens knows the novel cannot fix this. That is what makes him great rather than merely sentimental.
Mr. Jarndyce, I think, is Dickens's answer to that problem — imperfect as answers go.
He cannot reform Chancery. He cannot rescue Jo. But he can speak to Richard and Ada with this extraordinary candour:
"I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it."
No authority. No claims. Only fidelity offered freely — and that, Dickens suggests, is the only kind worth having.
And Jarndyce does something else in that scene that I find enormously touching.
He tells them he imagined their love — 'afar off,' he says, twice — as a real possibility.
"I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together."
That parenthesis — 'don't be shy, Ada' — just breaks your heart a little.
It's a man who loves these young people so much he can barely contain the tenderness even mid-sentence.
And perhaps that is where Bleak House leaves us — not with a solution, but with a question held in tension.
A system that produces Jo — nameless, friendless, educated by no one — and a household that produces Esther, Richard, Ada, Jarndyce.
The novel holds both. It refuses to let either cancel the other out.
Daniel, Edmund, Caroline — thank you. This has been exactly the kind of conversation the novel deserves.
For Bleak House Unpacked, I'm your host — and we'll see you next time.

c1:p1.text:
Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.
c1:p1.summary: Fog blankets London from the Thames to the marshes, penetrating every space and afflicting everyone from Greenwich pensioners to cabin boys, creating an all-encompassing sense of obscurity and misery.
c1:p1.best_quote: Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.

c6:p46.text:
The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.
c6:p46.summary: Detailed description of Bleak House's furnishings in each room, establishing a warm, hospitable environment filled with quirky collections and careful comfort.

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.
c7:p59.best_quote: I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!

c10:p66.text:
For, on a low bed opposite the fire, a confusion of dirty patchwork,
lean-ribbed ticking, and coarse sacking, the lawyer, hesitating just
within the doorway, sees a man. He lies there, dressed in shirt and
trousers, with bare feet. He has a yellow look in the spectral
darkness of a candle that has guttered down until the whole length of
its wick (still burning) has doubled over and left a tower of
winding-sheet above it. His hair is ragged, mingling with his
whiskers and his beard—the latter, ragged too, and grown, like the
scum and mist around him, in neglect. Foul and filthy as the room is,
foul and filthy as the air is, it is not easy to perceive what fumes
those are which most oppress the senses in it; but through the
general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco,
there comes into the lawyer’s mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium.
c10:p66.summary: Tulkinghorn discovers a man on a low, filthy bed—Nemo—dressed in shirt and trousers, spectral and yellowed, with long unkempt hair and whiskers, and the sickly air redolent of stale tobacco and opium.
c10:p66.best_quote: through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium

That graceless creature only knows that the dead man (whom he
recognized just now by his yellow face and black hair) was sometimes
hooted and pursued about the streets. That one cold winter night when
he, the boy, was shivering in a doorway near his crossing, the man
turned to look at him, and came back, and having questioned him and
found that he had not a friend in the world, said, “Neither have I.
Not one!” and gave him the price of a supper and a night’s lodging.
That the man had often spoken to him since and asked him whether he
slept sound at night, and how he bore cold and hunger, and whether he
ever wished to die, and similar strange questions. That when the man
had no money, he would say in passing, “I am as poor as you to-day,
Jo,” but that when he had any, he had always (as the boy most
heartily believes) been glad to give him some.
c11:p87.summary: Jo reveals the dead man recognized him, showed him kindness, asked about his welfare, and when poor himself, shared what little he had.

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.

subject so far removed from my Lady’s station.

c12:p114.best_quote: During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another—as was natural, perhaps, in the discussion of so unusual a subject...But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”
c13:p118.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.

c23:p37.text:
We walked a little way without speaking, and presently Richard
addressed me in his frankest and most feeling manner, thus: “My dear
Esther, I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant
sort of fellow. I don’t mean constant to Ada, for I love her
dearly—better and better every day—but constant to myself.
(Somehow, I mean something that I can’t very well express, but you’ll
make it out.) If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have
held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and
should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and
shouldn’t be in debt,  and—”
c23:p37.summary: Richard makes an earnest and heartfelt confession to Esther that he wishes he were more constant, both to himself and to his various professional pursuits, and admits his financial troubles.

Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don’t know that everybody
has two names. Never heerd of sich a think. Don’t know that Jo is
short for a longer name. Thinks it long enough for HIM. HE don’t find
no fault with it. Spell it? No. HE can’t spell it. No father, no
mother, no friends. Never been to school. What’s home? Knows a
broom’s a broom, and knows it’s wicked to tell a lie. Don’t recollect
who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both. Can’t
exactly say what’ll be done to him arter he’s dead if he tells a lie
to the gentlemen here, but believes it’ll be something wery bad to
punish him, and serve him right—and so he’ll tell the truth.

c13:p99.text:
There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.

c13:p113.text:
“Rick,” said Mr. Jarndyce, “I am glad to have won your confidence. I
hope to preserve it. When I contemplated these relations between us
four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new
interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the
possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don’t be shy, Ada,
don’t be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together.
I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was
afar off, Rick, afar off!”
c13:p113.summary: Mr. Jarndyce addresses Richard and Ada, confirming he is glad to have their confidence and that he did contemplate their union as a possibility.

I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!

c13:p115.text:
“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”
c13:p115.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.
